Messages.Author: ERIC SCOTT MANCH
Messages.Body:
I'm sure that a lot of people are going to jump down my throat for
this, because I seem to be going against the overwhelming sentiment
of the group, but I'm going to say it anyway. I've been lurking on
this newsgroup for some time now, and from the posts I've seen re-
garding the upcoming Sabbat expansion, I've just got to ask one
question: What on *earth* is everybody so upset about?
I've been a fan of V:TM and Jyhad for some time now, and I for
one appreciate the assiduousness with which WotC has attempted to
flesh out the WoD in the previous two expansions. Granted, some de-
cisions were made that were probably ill-advised (do any of us *really*
need boxes of Praxis Seizure: Londons?). On the whole, though, I feel
that WotC has made the game interesting and fluid. Now, the Sabbat
is upon us, and complaints about underpowered cards and vampires, es-
calation, and such have become even more ubiquitous than they usually
are. What do we make of all this?
Personally, I feel that 90% of this discourse is overheated
nonsense. Yes, Shotgun Ritual lets you play 2nd round thaumaturgy
strikes first round, and yes, Eldritch Glimmer does a heckuva lot of
damage, but at what cost? Gobs and gobs of blood. You can pump
all the blood you want into that superpowered strike, but you better
hope that your opponent doesn't slap down a Majesty, or worse, send
you to torpor (let's not even consider what Protean, Quietus, or agg.
damage in general can do). Yes, Thoughts Betrayed precludes this
possibility, but *geez* do you realistically plan to spend that much
blood? If you do, you can plan on changing your strategy very soon.
All of this speculation assumes that you have a large cap. vampire
that can pull all of this off-no Roreca Quaids need apply.
What about Tzimice, you ask? What about them? Most of their
strikes are quite impressive, granted, but they come at a hefty cost.
The NL environment of Jyhad prevents the Tzimisce, Tremere, etc. from
outright dominance. For every daunting strike you attempt to execute,
you must contend with the possibility of a S:CE. Malkavians? Hope
you can catch them with their stealth. Giovanni? You better be able
to contend with the spirits, or prevent them from beating the crap out
of you? Nosferatu? See Malks and Giovanni above. The list goes on
and on.
How about Walk through Arcadia? Keep in mind two things: 1.
it's rare, and 2. It's Antitribu-specific (I think). Without Dominate,
the Sabbat Malks need all the help they can get. And even if the card
isn't antitribu-specific, how many people are seriously going to assem-
ble a deck with 10 of these things? If someone tries, they seriously
need to reexamine their life. As for the rest-+1 on tham. strikes, Ian
Forestal, Gangrel with dom., whatever-the verdict will be the same. The
fundamental balance of the game remains untouched. A well-constructed
Ventrue vote deck will have a fair shot at beating a revved-up Tremere
Sabbat deck with pretty new strike cards any day of the week. Frankly,
I'm not too worried. So buy your new Sabbat decks and enjoy the game,
for chrissakes. If this new expansion is too much for you, then pick
up your cards and cry in the corner. The rest of us who take this game
less seriously will get along just fine.

--

While I agree that rarity is not a valid argument to justify a card's power
(the only major, to my mind, flaw with the Sabbat and, to a lesser extent,
Ancient Hearts), Walk's not as gross a way to render things unblockable
as some others in the cardset. Not that that justifies it either. Ever
since the original set, Unblockable Bleed has been feasible (without leaving
the Jyhad set, Tremere with Fortitude DayOp/Chantry or Ventrue DayOp/
FreakDrive/RapidHealing/FreakDrive/Restoration is quite bad already), and
has been made easiear with each expansion -- Dark Sovs brought Horrific
Countenance, Ancient Hearts brought Return to Innocence (which, by the way,
I support the fix for: "This action may not be modified." Shuts down the
Etrii deck right there. But I digress). By comparison, Walk through Arcadia
seems downright mild.

There's no 50% chance of failure with DayOp. Is a 50% failure rate an
acceptable tradeoff for a 100% go to torpor rate? An open question.

Note that AntiMalk don't shape up, with Dementation, as a bleed deck
primarily, but more a resource ravage deck -- hose allies, hose vampires,
without combat (or at least with nonstandard combat). Coma's gross on
first view, but with a well-designed deck, you either hate combat and can
usually avoid it, or you love combat and usually outfight it. And if you
can't sometimes, then hey. That just means it's a viable card.

to the game than Ancient Hearts, which is to say, it's nontrivially crocked,

addition.

What was really, REALLY bad about AH? Return to Innocence. Modulo that
and the piss-poor job done on Serpentis (Form of Corruption should have
been an uncommon, and Tongue of the Serpent is just garbage), the set is
quite nice. But I digress, again.

It *IS* possible to do a good job, and the Sabbat's not quite there, agreed.
But Gehenna it ain't. People are overreacting. Mind you, they're underreacting
as well, albeit with less volume.

>Really? You don't think rush/thoughts betrayed is a problem?

I know *I* don't. I'm regarded, in my own group, as a premier deckbuilder.
I can't make a combat deck that abuses Thoughts Betrayed. I've tried.
I've made decks that have been regarded as borderline degenerate, currently
the Golfball deck (so many Dimples!) that breeds 2point Obfuscating weenies
in disgusting quantity. But I can't make the dreaded eeevil Thoughts Betrayed

Messages.Author: Paul J. Lareau
Messages.Body:
ERIC SCOTT MANCH wrote:
> I'm sure that a lot of people are going to jump down my throat for
> this, because I seem to be going against the overwhelming sentiment
> of the group, but I'm going to say it anyway. I've been lurking on
> this newsgroup for some time now, and from the posts I've seen re-
> garding the upcoming Sabbat expansion, I've just got to ask one
> question: What on *earth* is everybody so upset about?

Thanks, Eric ... allow another lurker to be someone who DOESN'T try to bleed you
through your tonsils! In fact, I'll probably do a major venom deflection in my own
direction.

In my short time playing V:tES (and very long time as a gamer), it seems to me that
there are three kinds of players, and this actually applies to pretty much all the
CCG's, although the arguments tend to get bloodier here than elsewhere.

First, there are the TOURNAMENT PLAYERS and WANNABEES. They tend to own boxes and
boxes of cards, and spend a great deal of money buying individual power cards and many
duplicates, so they see little fun in any card limit games. They delight in disputing
the rules, tend to be very conservative about changes in the game, and tend to play
for blood (uhhh, bad choice of words!). They are also probably the best players, have
the most serious attitude toward gaming, and do a great deal to keep the game
companies on the "straight and narrow". These folks join a long tradition of serious
chess, bridge, and wargame players.

Secondly, there are the FUN or PARTY PLAYERS. They tend to own far fewer cards, and
probably play many different games, both CCG and others. As a result, they see CL
games as a protection against the "big guys", but the issue isn't a big one with them.
Most of their sessions include at least a neonate or two, so they often tend to
interpret rules simply and liberally, with lots of informal agreements, which makes
the rule lawyers crazy! They like it when the game companies make changes and add
concepts, and are anxious to try new things. These folks tend to come out of the
non-CCG card and board games world, tend to be a bit older, and may have even gotten
turned on to games by playing with their kids.

Thirdly, there are the STORYTELLER or AESTHETIC PLAYERS and COLLECTORS. They tend to
have lots of cards, read many articles on the background of the game, are fans of the
artwork, and tend to play a small group of games, usually theme-based like Sci-Fi,
Horror, Anime, etc. They also tend to like games with card limits, and in fact some
even like to play closed deck or modified closed deck games. They tend to play with
others of their kind, their constructed decks are virtually always theme decks, and
they are known to omit certain powerful cards from their decks because "a Toreador
wouldn't do anything that plebean, and besides the picture on the card doesn't fit my
theme". This drives the serious players absolutely malky! They also tend to like to
continue a running commentary on what "actually has happened in the story" when they
play a card. These folks usually have a background in D&D or other RPG's, and also
tend to write lots of articles, stories, and are frequently Internet afficianados.

The problem is that while these 3 kinds of folks seldom encounter each other playing
the game, they run into each other (violently!) in the newsgroup, and don't realize
they are playing three different games. Perhaps WoTC should publish more sets of
alternate rules to appeal to these different types of players. Individual players do
indeed rewrite the rules and come up with some great games.

--

Nathan Harada writes:
> My question is: How does your playgroup deal with newbies? Do
>you get very many? How do you get them to a level where they can
>compete with the others in the group?

We used to get newbies, but not many anymore. We get them to a
"competitive level" by plying with them and expalining how decks work.

> To Everybody: How do you teach Jyhad strategy to newbies?

Normally, we loan them effective but simple decks (S&B, rush combat,
intercept combat, heavy vote decks, etc.). I prefer to loan aggressive
and transient-oriented decks. Far and away the most common error when
people are learning Jyhad is that they overemphasize permanents and
defense and underestimate the importance of speed and timing; it helps for
them to see the other ways to handle things in Jyhad.

This is definately true, but what I find frustrating as an 'old'
player of Jyhad, is that; while the newbies pick up the rules of
the game quite quickly, it takes them a lot longer to figure out
the tactics needed to build decks and play with the decks
effectively. This leads to games involving newbies to be onesided
if one of us more experianced player is there predator or prey,
due to the fact that there decks tend to get crushed quite
quickly. This is also frustrating for the newbie as he gets fed
up of being crushed time and time again and a lot of
encouragement is needed to keep them playing. I always give help
when needed and find the best way to decrease this early trauma
is to create a deck with the newbie, using his desired clans, and
talk him through the design stages of the deck. This normally
guarantees a semi-competative deck from the start. Once the
newbie has picked up hints and tactics through playing then he
can modify or make his own deck as required, hell he may even win
a few....
